articles.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
articles.author: Grace Huckins
articles.body_markdown:
METR’s latest report finds that AI models are still improving at a rapid clip, but they show some weaknesses in tasks that require judgment.

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify \[tasks\].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

articles.title: Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead
articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.body_markdown:
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized.

Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

**Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence**The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

"The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."

Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.

Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.

Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

**Terror in Sinaloa**Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.

Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.

"The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.

Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.

**Capture prompts celebration and warnings**Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."

Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

Five experienced researchers, including a Nobel prizewinner, revisit the dead ends, bloopers and moments of stubborn certainty that shaped their science.

To err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” says Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

## PETER SHAWHAN: Learning to find nothing is a skill

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

For the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

In the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise showed a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them quickly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is important; it’s a real scientific skill.

## OMAR YAGHI: A fixed mindset is the enemy of discovery

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

Back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

Then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

articles.title: Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?
articles.author: Steven Strogatz; Janna Levin
articles.body_markdown:
## Introduction

Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared architectural features that their components alone could not explain. This suggested common organizing principles for how networks form and develop.

In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name. The conversation then turns to health and nutrition. Disease-related genes cluster in “network neighborhoods”, Barabási explains, which may help identify better drug targets and predict which patients will respond to which drugs. That work led him to his Foodome project, which catalogs the molecules found in the food we eat and asks what they do inside our cells. By his count, around 135,000 compounds lie outside conventional nutrition, which concerns itself mainly with energy, building blocks, and vitamins. These compounds, which he calls the “dark matter of nutrition,” and their effects on the body are only beginning to be understood.

Listen on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, TuneIn or your favorite podcasting app, or you can stream it from Quanta.

##  **Transcript**

**STEVE STROGATZ:** Hello, I’m Steve Strogatz.

**JANNA LEVIN:** And I’m Janna Levin.

**STROGATZ:** And this is *The Joy of Why*.

**LEVIN:** A podcast… where… you can’t make me laugh, okay. A podcast from *Quanta Magazine* where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

**STROGATZ:** Well, hey, Janna, I’m gonna take you back in a time warp to the 1990s. Do you wanna go there with me?

**LEVIN:** Yeah, for sure.

**STROGATZ:** There was a trend back then, where people would play a game that they called Six Degrees of Separation.

**LEVIN:** Yeah, it was like the Kevin Bacon game.

**STROGATZ:** Right. So if people don’t remember, Kevin Bacon, he was in a lot of movies and a game developed around him where you would name an actor, whoever, Marlon Brando or James Dean, and then you have to figure out a path of co-stars. You know, Marlon Brando was in such and such movie with somebody who was in a movie with Kevin Bacon. In that case, we would say Marlon Brando was two steps away. He had a Bacon number of two.

**LEVIN:** \[*Laughs*\] Right. Now, this though has some actual mathematical underpinnings. And as I remember, you did substantial work on some of this, how we’re all connected and how the world is smaller than we think, how that happens. You know, how do you… Do you know the guy Joe from Chicago? And you’re like, “Of course I know Joe.” Right?

**STROGATZ:** Well, it is true. My student Duncan Watts and I got very interested in the math of Six Degrees of Separation, like what would a network have to be like to have that property? And around that time, when we published our paper, soon after we heard from Malcolm Gladwell before he was really famous as Malcolm Gladwell, and he wanted to talk about this idea, and he ended up writing an article that was called Six Degrees of Lois Weisberg.

**LEVIN:** Sure, I know Lois.

**STROGATZ:** Yeah, that’s the point. Everybody knows Lois. Lois knew everyone in Chicago and all over the place.

And so, we all know that there are these connectors in our networks, and that’s actually what we’re gonna be hearing about to some extent in this upcoming interview with László Barabási.

So, he is a network scientist at Northeastern University. He’s also got an appointment with Harvard Medical School and with the Central European University in Budapest, Hungary. And he has been looking at the role of what he calls hubs. You know, these outsized Lois Weisberg-like nodes in a network that seem to have a tremendous number of connections and the effect that they have on the behavior of the network as a result.

**LEVIN:** This probably has application for other complex systems than just human social systems?

**STROGATZ:** Oh, it certainly does. Understanding networks, not just from the perspective of human social life, has had all kinds of consequences for our understanding of how diseases spread through populations, but also how brains are wired together. The way genes are connected in gene regulation networks, or even the power plants that provide energy to all our homes and businesses.

So, yeah, very big implications way beyond human society. So, for that, let’s turn to one of the experts. Here we go with László Barabási.

\[*Music plays*\]

**STROGATZ:** Welcome to *The Joy of Why*, László.

**ALBERT-LÁSZLÓ BARABÁSI:** Oh, Steve, this is so much fun. I am a big listener of podcast, and *Joy of Why* is actually on my active list, so it’s so much fun to kind of see the sauce being made.

**STROGATZ:** \[*Laughs*\] Well, it’s great to have you here. So just for full disclosure to our listeners, we have known each other a long time. It must be close to 30 years by now. I’d like to begin by going down memory lane with you to the early days of network theory. You spent a lot of your career looking at the world through the lens of networks. Why don’t you start by telling us what we mean by networks, and also what looking at the world this way offers us?

**BARABÁSI:** Well, you forgot to disclose the fact that we were responsible, you and I, for the field of network science, right? So we were once competitors, too. But let’s talk about why I think both of us cared about the networks at that time. Because fundamentally, nothing exists in isolation, right? A gene, a neuron, a human doesn’t make sense at all to kind of think about them in isolation. They all start making sense when they connect to other things. So consciousness is really about what the neurons do together. Life is what our genes and molecules do together. Society is what we do together.

And if we tend to focus, as much of science did historically, on the pieces, we are actually missing the why. Why do we have intelligence? Why do we have life? Why do we have societies?

**STROGATZ:** A-ha. So it’s this relational perspective. You’re pushing back against the usual straw man of reductionism, it sounds like.

**BARABÁSI:** Don’t we all, right? Because, I mean, listen. Reductionism is a key tool in science, right? Without that, we cannot do networks. We need to know the pieces.

But we as scientists got so busy looking at the parts that we have forgotten the whole thing. And then network science is really one of the disciplines whose starting point you gotta map out how things are connected and why that matters.

**STROGATZ:** It’s interesting you talk about mapping things out, because back in the 1990s, especially towards the second half of the 1990s, each of us with our students wrote papers that made a big splash. That’s what you’re referring to when you speak of us starting the subject.

But what do you think was known at the time we were starting and what was not known? What was it we collectively were trying to figure out?

**BARABÁSI:** Yeah. So I think none of us discovered networks, right? Networks were there for a long, long time, and many disciplines were aware of that, right? And I think in my mind, two things have changed.

One of them is the availability of data, right? Our ability to take advantage of the revolution that was really brought to us by the internet to really start putting the pieces together and create the maps of how metabolites in the cell are connected to each other, how actors in Hollywood — your work, right — are connected to each other through common movies and so on.

And so one really opportunity that we all took advantage is the availability of the data. But then that by itself, in my mind, would have not been sufficient, right? Because if data becomes available, we could still have a theory of biological networks and a theory of social networks and difference.

The key discovery that we and others had made at that time is once we look from the network perspective of these systems, there are many more similarities in the architecture of real systems than differences. And I think that was surprising to all of us because I don’t have to convince anybody that a metabolic network within the cell should be different from a social network or should be different from the wiring of the brain. They have totally different purpose, totally different scale, totally different units who are being connected in different ways of interactions.

So what really shocked many of us physicists, mathematicians, biologists, is that many of these networks have common architectural features that could not be simply explained by the nature of the nodes and the links or the nature of the components, but it was hinting to some deeper organizing principles that governs connectedness.

**STROGATZ:** That’s very well expressed. That’s nice. This is a field, as you remember, and I certainly do, there’s a question of turf. You know, there are people, for instance, in pure math, who will say, “Don’t tell me networks are new. We’ve been doing graph theory since the Königsberg bridge problem with Leonhard Euler sometime in the 1700s.”

But so, what are some of the differences in philosophy and content between, say, this subject and the older subjects, let’s just to pick two, graph theory and social networks?

**BARABÁSI:** Of course. We are very grateful to many of our colleagues, the Erdős and Rényi and the László Lovász of mathematics and the Milgrams and the Manfred Kochens of social networks and so on, because they really been using graph theory to look at various issues related to connectedness.

I think the fundamental difference was that on one end, graph theorists never really bothered or were interested to look at real networks. Social network theorists, however, were limited to very, very small networks. And once the data became available on other networks, from biological to very large social networks, we started features that simply could not be observed at those smaller samples.

And most important — and I think this was the key — we and everybody realized that the models that the field has built up, for instance, the 1950s to pretty much the end of 1990s, were not sufficient to describe the reality of these systems. So there was a need for a very, very different way of thinking about that.

What was missing is that graph theory and social networks were using graphs as kind of cartographers to map out what’s out there, but they were not thinking so much about how things came into being. Why are networks the way they are? That is, networks are not static objects. They are dynamical entities that evolve in time. The large networks we see are the result of massive growth processes and how this temporal evolution, how these dynamics defines the way they look, their architecture, and their ability to do things, which is being alive, to think, to function as a system.

**STROGATZ:** That’s a really nice point that there is this temporal aspect which was not particularly the concern of traditional graph theory. You know, now we all just talk about the internet, but to us in the ’90s, the World Wide Web was a shocking thing.

This is before social media. There was no Facebook. This was just web pages on the internet. There was a browser called Mozilla that came on around 1994, if I remember right, and you could start to do the thing that we called web surfing. So you started to have this visceral sensation of hopping from page to page through this vast, mysterious, hard-to-picture structure and you did some of the first work pioneering what it was like to navigate and explore this amazing, weird virtual world that didn’t exist until the ’90s. As you say, it’s like cartography, exploring a whole new world.

**BARABÁSI:** I’m glad you mentioned that because this unlocked network science for us. As a historical note, I wrote my first network paper in 1995 that never got published. It’s still there on the archive. And ’95 and ’96, I spent trying to convince computer scientists to help me map out the World Wide Web, and no one bothered to respond.

I have sent countless emails to people who were building, like, robots at that time. We didn’t call them search engine. We called them robots and crawlers, and just asking for their data, and no one bothered to respond. It wasn’t ’til 1998 when How Hong Jon, my postdoc, who had a very strong programming skill came along, that we could actually finally embark on that project and map it out.

And let me give you a little historical anecdote even for the listeners to indicate what kind of world was that. So right after we mapped the World Wide Web and our paper came out in ’99, I was immediately invited to the Internet Archives in San Francisco to give a talk, and there were about 10 of us speakers there, right?

And there was a guy who came along, and he put a big box on the table and said, “You know, I just funded a company, and why don’t you just take my T-shirt?” And the T-shirt said Google on it. It was Larry Page handing out, as a graduate student, his first T-shirts actually.

**STROGATZ:** Wow.

**BARABÁSI:** So, the fundamental difference between what we did and Larry Page did is that we just mapped out the network and not the content, and he, of course, cared about the content. And of course, that difference turned out to be a couple of trillion dollars in the long run. But nevertheless, these were the roots of how do we think about internet, World Wide Web, and so on as interconnected systems that, as you said, they are so natural to us that we don’t any longer even think about that.

**STROGATZ:** Right, it was a mind-blowing thing at the time. And you made this point earlier that I wanna return to about growth, that the network of the World Wide Web, but also whether it’s biological networks or even a city starting from a small village, networks are not static. They grow, they accrete, they add nodes, they add connections, links. And you had the nice idea that very simple observation, that networks grow, might leave a signature of some kind on their structure. blocks.text: Introduction

Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared architectural features that their components alone could not explain. This suggested common organizing principles for how networks form and develop.

In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name. The conversation then turns to health and nutrition. Disease-related genes cluster in “network neighborhoods”, Barabási explains, which may help identify better drug targets and predict which patients will respond to which drugs. That work led him to his Foodome project, which catalogs the molecules found in the food we eat and asks what they do inside our cells. By his count, around 135,000 compounds lie outside conventional nutrition, which concerns itself mainly with energy, building blocks, and vitamins. These compounds, which he calls the “dark matter of nutrition,” and their effects on the body are only beginning to be understood.

articles.title: Our solar system’s doomsday may come sooner than we thought
articles.author: Phil Plait
articles.body_markdown:
I’m starting to really wonder just how stable our solar system really is.

To be clear, I’m not worried about planets being flung away into interstellar space any time soon. But “soon” means something different to an astronomer than it does to a normal person. Millions of years is “soon.” A few billion? Now that’s a bit later.

Fail to factor in deep time, though, and it’s all too easy to mistakenly think that the solar system is static, that it has always been as it is now. After all, it *looks* well ordered. The inner four planets are all small and rocky, while the outer four are swollen giants with thick atmospheres, and a belt of asteroids splits the two types like a demarcation zone.

But things are not as they appear. One clue turned up when astronomers found the first exoplanets orbiting sunlike stars in the 1990s. These were “hot Jupiters,” gas giants akin to our solar system’s biggest planet but huddled in orbits far closer to their stars than Mercury is to our own. They could not have formed there, so astronomers postulated they were instead born farther out and gradually migrated inward via gravitational interactions with the same circumstellar disk of material from which they first coalesced.

The hot Jupiters were only an early wave of weird worlds. In some other systems, planets orbit on wildly tilted trajectories, and, here and there, astronomers have found planets that actually revolve around their host stars *backward*. These oddities imply some sort of chaotic interaction at work, such as planets perturbing each other as they pass by and getting tossed into bizarre configurations.

Then, in 2005, scientists proposed what is now called the Nice model (after the French city where the scientists met and developed the idea). This radical hypothesis is that the solar system’s giant planets formed closer to the sun than their present positions, only to migrate outward to their current arrangement as a result of gravitational tussles with each other. The Nice model, and its many subsequent modifications, brought the “migratory” view of planets home, and this key insight has been a staple of solar system dynamics ever since.

I consider planetary migration’s place in celestial mechanics as similar to the role of evolution in biology or plate tectonics in geology: *nothing* makes sense unless you include it. It’s the framework of how we understand the way planetary orbits evolve.

It also strongly implies these changes are ongoing. The solar system *continues* to evolve.

In one sense, we already knew this to be true: The sun won’t last forever. As I wrote in my September 18, 2026, Universe column, in six billion years or so, changes in our star’s core will lead to it swelling up and becoming a red giant. The puffed-up sun will slowly shed its outer layers, causing its mass to decrease and its gravity to weaken, and in response, the planets will gradually move farther out from it. Some astronomers had previously assumed that this relatively gentle process meant the outer solar system planets would orbit stably for immense periods of time, possibly as much as 100 billion years—long after the sun itself is quite dead.

There’s evidence that suggests the sun’s future evolution won’t be a smooth, sedate process, though: instabilities in its core will result in episodic paroxysms in which our star’s luminosity will briefly increase drastically. These sporadic stellar spasms will cause the sun to lose mass in powerful but brief *pulses* instead of in a smooth flow.

And there’s more: research into how the sun loses that mass shows that it won’t be blown off symmetrically in all directions. Instead each pulse will send material off *asymmetrically*, in a relatively random direction, like a sudden gust of wind.

If this is indeed the case, it will a have profound impact on the far future of the solar system.

A team of astronomers looked into this and published its results on September 21 in the *Astrophysical Journal Letters*. The researchers simulated how the sun will lose mass over the course of several billion years—from when it starts to become a red giant to the inevitable end of the process, in which it loses all its outer layers, exposing its core to space. At that point it will be a white dwarf, a hot, dense ball with about half the current solar mass but squeezed into a volume only about the size of Earth.

In their simulations, they assumed that the solar mass loss will occur in a series of thousands of small burps, each one ejecting about 0.01 percent of the sun’s material into space. Also, these solar eructations will form a broad funnel shape instead of expanding spherically.

That last bit is critical. By focusing the emitted material, the ejection acts like a rocket, pushing on the sun. The amount of force imparted is relatively small, only enough to give it a very small kick. But this does accelerate our star, each adding a few meters per second to its velocity in space.

Each kick is in a random direction. Now, you might think this would average out to zero net force acting on the sun, but that’s not the case. This situation mimics that of a “random walk,” in which taking a step in a random direction slowly leads away from your starting point. After a finite number of steps, you’ll have moved in some direction as if pushed there. In the same way, random ejections of matter can push a star in some overall direction as well, leading to the final velocity of several kilometers per second.

This may not seem like much, but it will actually have a big effect on the planets.

Well, not the *inner* planets so much—we already know what happens to them, and it’s nothing good. Mercury and Venus will be consumed by the expanding sun. Earth may escape that fate, but both it and Mars will be broiled as our star grows enormous.

But, according to the new work, the outer planets don’t fare much better.

In practical terms, as these kicks push around the sun, the planets’ orbits around it become more elongated. In a disturbing 77 percent of the simulations, the outer planets migrate so much because of this mass loss that eventually one crosses the orbit of another—and this happens early on in the process. In at least one case, Saturn is lost within just a few million years of the sun becoming a red giant! These gravitational encounters lead to ejected planets or system disruptions in *40 percent* of the simulations, long before the sun even becomes a white dwarf. After three billion years, total disruption occurs in a staggering 90 percent of the simulations.

Previously astronomers thought that as the sun died and the orbits of the planets expanded, nearby passes of other stars would eventually disrupt the solar system after many tens of billions of years. This new work indicates that by the time these close encounters happen, there won’t be much of a solar system left to disrupt.

That’s a little depressing. If there’s an upside, it’s that this won’t happen for many billions of years from now. As far as we can tell, the planets—including our own—will be fine for eons to come.

But if you have plans for seven or eight billion years hence, you might want to reassess them.
